bio.en: Molly Graham is an operating executive who has worked with founder-CEOs like Mark Zuckerberg, Sheryl Sandberg, Larry Page, and Sergey Brin, and coined the "give away your Legos" framework.
bio.zh: 莫莉·格雷厄姆（Molly Graham）是一位运营高管，曾与马克·扎克伯格、谢丽尔·桑德伯格、拉里·佩奇、谢尔盖·布林等创始人型 CEO 共事，并首创了"交出你的乐高"（give away your Legos）框架。

summary.en: Molly argues that ~80% of company culture is defined by the founder's personality, and leaders must articulate and scale it deliberately. She introduces "giving away your Legos" - letting go of what you're good at to take on new challenges as the company grows. The episode also covers the J-curve versus stairs model of career risk and growth.
summary.zh: 莫莉认为，约 80% 的公司文化由创始人的个性决定，领导者必须有意识地去阐释并放大它。她提出"交出你的乐高"——在公司成长时，放下你擅长的事，去迎接新挑战。本期还涵盖了职业风险与成长的"J 曲线 vs 阶梯"模型。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: So first of all, Ami Vora, who you have had on your podcast, once said to me that all advice is just someone telling you what they did. And I always think about that. Because I really think that basically what I tell people is I've made every single mistake in the book. And then I got to the end of the book and I started inventing new mistakes. So mostly what I feel is that I like sharing my stories because I want to help people. I want to help people not make the same mistakes I did. And I also want to help people make sense of what they're experiencing. But I started in tech in 2007. I actually started at Google the week the iPhone launched and a lot of my scaling battle scars come from a couple of experiences. They come from a year and a half at Google, which is not very long. (00:06:17): And Google was pretty big when I was there. It has thousands of employees. But my department, which was the communications department, was 25 people when I joined and it grew in nine months to 125 people. And that was really my first experience with just all the sort of things that I still talk about today. In terms of what it feels like to grow really, really fast and sort of all the tools that I started developing from there. After Google, I left and followed Cheryl Sandberg and Elliot Schrage to Facebook. And I spent five years at Facebook. And I joined Facebook in 2008, and it's important context because it was 80 million users at the time. We were smaller than MySpace. It was 270 million in revenue, 500 employees. It did not feel inevitable. Most people thought we were going to sell it to Microsoft. When I told people I was going there, they were like, isn't that place just like a site for college kids? And so I was there for five years and it was a crazy five years. (00:07:22): When I left, it was 5,500 employees, five billion in revenue, over a billion users. So a huge amount of what I experienced, what I write about, what I talk about in Glue Club, which is the community that I run, comes from that rapid scale at Google and Facebook. But I also, I left Facebook right after we went public, about six months after we went public. And I only like doing jobs that I'm highly unqualified for. I like being on learning curves so steep that I'm scared I'm going to fall off. And so I left and I wanted to learn what it took to build something from nothing. And so I joined this little startup founded by Brett Taylor, a startup called Quip. I joined a couple of months before we launched and ran everything that wasn't product and engineering there for him. (00:08:27): And it really taught me about all the tools and skills you need to go from zero to one and then from one to two and how lonely it can be to build something. And we eventually sold that company to Salesforce. And then again, only take jobs I'm highly unqualified for. But the last really chaotic scaling experience I had was actually helping Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan start their philanthropy, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. And I basically helped them for the first two years of its existence or its sort of like first full existence. And philanthropy sounds calm. You know what I mean? We're like, oh, giving money away. Must be so peaceful over there. And CZI grew from, I think the week I joined, it was 30 people and we bought two companies that week and it grew to 250 people that year. And it was like using every single tool in my toolkit that I had taken from every other job that I'd had. (00:09:22): So my advice and frameworks, like I said, come from having made a lot of mistakes. But I've also sort of made a personal study over the last 18 years, believe it or not. Essentially what does it take to thrive inside growing and changing companies, not just to hang on for dear life. What does it take to lead in the face of constant change? 首先，曾做客我播客的阿米·沃拉（Ami Vora）曾对我说过，所有建议不过是别人把自己走过的路告诉你。我对此深有感触，因为我觉得自己给别人的建议，无非就是把自己犯过的所有错误都罗列一遍。等我学完一遍教训后，又开始创造新的错误。所以我觉得分享自己的故事很重要——一方面是为了帮助别人，避免他们重蹈我的覆辙；另一方面，也是为了让人们能理解自己正在经历的困境。但我2007年入行科技行业时，可谓一波三折。事实上，iPhone发布那周我就加入了谷歌，之后的扩张历程留下了许多宝贵的经验教训。（00:06:17）：当时谷歌规模庞大，我加入的通信部门仅有25人，却在9个月内扩展至125人。这段经历让我深刻体会到快速扩张的挑战，以及由此催生的诸多管理工具。离开谷歌后，我追随谢丽尔·桑德伯格和埃利奥特·施拉格加入Facebook，并在那里度过了五年时光。2008年加入Facebook时，公司仅有8000万用户，规模远小于MySpace，营收2.7亿美元，员工500人。当时外界普遍认为我们会被微软收购。当我告诉别人要去Facebook时，他们质疑“这不就是个大学生玩的社交网站吗？”这五年堪称疯狂之旅。（00:07:22）：离开时Facebook已拥有5500名员工，营收50亿美元，用户超10亿。谷歌和Facebook的快速扩张经历，是我如今分享经验、撰写文章、运营Glue Club社群的重要源泉。但在Facebook上市六个月后，我选择离开，只因我偏爱挑战极限的工作环境。于是我加入了布雷特·泰勒创立的初创公司Quip，参与了产品与工程之外的所有事务。这段经历让我深刻体会到从零到一，再从一到二的创业历程，以及独自开创事业的孤独感。最终我们将公司出售给Salesforce。最后一次混乱的扩张经历，是协助马克·扎克伯格和普莉希拉·陈创立慈善机构Chan Zuckerberg Initiative。在其成立初期，我深度参与了两年的运营。人们总以为慈善事业轻松自在，但实际上，面对快速扩张的压力，能坚持下去的人实在太少了。
那一年有250个人参与其中。当时，我仿佛动用了自己从其他工作中积累的所有技能和经验。（00:09:22）所以，正如我所说，我的建议和框架都源自于我犯过的诸多错误。但说实话，在过去的18年里，我也一直在进行自我探索。归根结底，要想在不断发展与变革的公司中蓬勃发展，而不只是勉强维持生存，需要具备哪些能力？面对持续的变革，如何发挥领导力？另一个让我深感兴趣的问题是，企业在发展后陷入停滞与那些能持续数代人的传奇企业之间，究竟有何本质区别？比如Twitter和MySpace与Facebook的差异——前者营收数十亿美元，后者则达到数千亿美元。于是，我希望能将自己的经验转化为对其他领导者的帮助，为人们提供切实有效的工具，同时坦诚地告诉大家，这一切的实现之路何其艰辛。

I got this. It's a house. All right, great. And then you're like, I'm good at building houses. I was put on earth to build houses. And almost assuredly inside of scaling companies, as soon as you're like, I feel good at this and I should do this forever. Somebody's going to show up and be like, okay, it's not a house. It's a neighborhood. And you need to take this house that's kind of half built and you're going to pass it off to this other person that we just hired. And you are going to go build dog parks and streets and other things that are entirely unhouse-like. And what happens when someone does that to you is you're like, wait a minute. First of all, I'm not done with this house. And I'm worried that this person's going to screw it up. (00:13:18): I'm also worried that building houses is actually the most fun thing and that I'm going to give the Legos to that person and they're going to have all the fun work and I'm going to hate building dog parks. Or that dog parks are irrelevant eventually and it's going to turn out we're in the house building business. So there's this incredible set of emotions that come territorialistic, paired with excitement. Fear paired with joy. But eventually you pass the house off and then you go work on neighborhoods and you're sort of like, okay, dog parks, I'm good at dog parks. I got this. And then again, you get to the like, I'm great. I was put on earth to build neighborhoods. And immediately someone shows up and says, it's not a neighborhood. It's a country or a city or a world. And it just goes on and on and on. (00:14:03): And for me, learning this muscle of both learning to give away what you've gotten good at and move on to the next shiny pile of Legos. And learning that the emotions associated with that are inevitable. I've been doing this for 18, 20 years, I still get attacked by these emotions all the time, but that doesn't mean that you shouldn't give them away and move on to the next thing. (00:14:33): That is both the torment of scaling companies, which is that the ground is moving under your feet. And as soon as you're comfortable, someone will make sure that you are uncomfortable, but it's also the opportunity, which is that you can go from being someone that's good at building houses to someone that knows how to build entire worlds. And that is where the Legos metaphor came from.
turns.zh:
这一切都始于我在谷歌的经历。后来在Facebook，简直就是在大规模发放乐高积木的过程。但我喜欢用这个比喻来形容它——当我看着领导者和员工们经历快速扩张时，我总觉得有人把一大堆乐高积木摆在一群幼儿园孩子面前，然后说，你们自己搭吧。刚开始的时候，你会觉得，天哪，积木太多了，太有趣了，机会多多，但又有点害怕和不知所措。你会想，积木太多了，该怎么下手？说明书不会藏在积木堆里吧？但你开始搭建后，就慢慢找到节奏，感觉自己在盖房子，掌握了窍门。然后，你会觉得自己擅长盖房子，简直是为盖房而生的。但在扩张型公司里，当你刚开始得意洋洋时，总会有人跳出来说：好吧，这不是盖房子，而是建社区。你得把这栋半成品的房子交给新招的员工，自己去搭狗狗公园和街道之类与盖房毫无关系的东西。当这种情况发生时，你会瞬间抓狂：等等，我还没搭完这栋房子呢！我担心别人会把它毁了！我又担心盖房才是最有趣的，乐高积木全被别人抢走了！或者狗狗公园根本不重要，最后发现我们还是在盖房子。这种情绪的起伏真是难以置信——既有领地意识，又夹杂着兴奋，恐惧又夹杂着喜悦。但最终你还是得把房子交出去，去搭建社区，然后又会觉得，狗狗公园我也擅长，我能行。接着又会自我膨胀，觉得自己是天生建社区的料。可紧接着又有人跳出来说：这不是社区，而是国家或城市，甚至是整个世界。这种循环永无止境。

对我来说，关键在于学会把擅长的事物拱手相让，转而投入下一堆闪亮的乐高积木。同时要明白，伴随这种转变的情绪波动是不可避免的。我从事这行18、20年，至今仍会被这些情绪反复折磨，但这并不意味着我们不能放手去做下一件事。

（00:14:03）
这就是扩张型公司的魔力所在——地面总在脚下移动。当你刚适应环境，别人就确保你再度陷入不安。但这也是机遇所在——你能从擅长盖房子，成长为能建造整个世界的专家。这正是乐高比喻的精髓所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a good metaphor. And if you've gone through this, you so understand what this is like and what... And also just the Legos is metaphor is so good for the different things you build.
turns.zh: 这个比喻太妙了。如果你经历过这些，就会深切体会其中的滋味……而乐高这个比喻用来形容你搭建的不同事物也太贴切了。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I have a very weird brain that for some odd reason just always thinks in metaphors.
turns.zh: 我的大脑结构很奇特，不知为何，总爱用比喻思考问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:15:11].

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: So it showed up when I was... At Facebook in particular, I would find that every so often I would have to have what I called a Legos talk with someone where I would just see them start to ask these questions like, why are we hiring that person? Or what's that team even do? And I was like, okay, we need to have the chat about the Legos. And then eventually it turned into an article and a whole thing.
turns.zh: 这在Facebook工作时就显现出来了。我经常需要和同事进行所谓的“乐高谈话”，比如他们会问：“为什么要招这个人？”或者“这个团队到底做什么的？” 这时我就想，好吧，我们得来一场“乐高对话”。最后这段对话还写成了一篇文章，引发了热议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A whole thing. And just to be clear, the advice is give away your Legos, this is actually the path to a successful career.
turns.zh: 引发了热议。说真的，我的建议是把你的“乐高积木”分享出去，这才是通往成功事业的正确路径。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I have watched a lot of people over many years struggle with feeling like they should hang on to the thing that they've been good at. And it almost always... Because, you know, essentially the nature of a scaling company is that the Lego pile is just getting bigger and bigger and bigger however fast that graph is going up into the right. I always say that's the graph of how fast your business is growing. It's the graph of how fast your company is expanding. And it's the graph of how fast your job is getting bigger. That means that if you actually just stay and build houses, eventually you're literally buried under a pile of Legos. Do you know what I mean? You held onto something that's down here and the opportunity is actually to stay on top of that pile and to learn to just give away your job every so often. (00:16:27): At Facebook, I got to a place where I was literally giving away my job every three weeks. I was constantly rehiring myself essentially because you have to sort of grow as fast as your company is growing if you really want to take advantage of the opportunity that comes with companies that are growing and changing quickly.
turns.zh:
多年来，我目睹许多人纠结于是否该固守自己擅长的领域。但几乎每次……因为，规模化公司的本质是乐高积木堆越堆越高——无论业务增长图表如何飙升。我常说，这图表代表了你的事业发展速度、公司扩张速度，以及你的职位晋升速度。若你固守原地，最终会被乐高积木埋没。懂我的意思吗？你紧握着地面上的积木，而真正的机遇在于站在堆顶，学会适时放手。
(00:16:27): 在Facebook，我每三周就会主动放下手头工作，重新寻找挑战。毕竟，要想抓住快速成长公司的机遇，就必须与公司同步发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So people are hearing this, they're like, okay, my rational brain's like, I should give away my Legos. It'll help me. It'll be good for my career. In real life, it's very hard to actually do. To give away this empire that you've built, this team that you've built. This project that you're like, oh, this is going to be my thing. I know you have a really fun, useful tool to help people deal with that kind of irrational part of their brain. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 听众听完后会想：好吧，我的理性脑告诉我该放下乐高积木，这对事业有益。但现实中要做到却难如登天——割舍亲手打造的帝国、团队，放弃视为心血的项目。想必你有妙招帮助人们克服这种非理性思维。请分享一下。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: So like I said, my brain works in weird metaphors. It's a weird brain. I was raised on The Muppets, and I like to think that this one came from, I guess, growing up watching weird animals. But basically, at some point I realized that this emotional rollercoaster that comes with scaling, with growing. With going through change, any kind of change. People feel that. Was never going to go away. And that no matter how good I got... Sometimes I think it gets worse the more senior you get, actually. Because you sort of feel like you're supposed to know what you're doing, and then you just get attacked by this monster that's like, who even gave you this job in the first place? So basically I externalized all these emotions that come with change into this little tiny monster. I named my monster, Bob. Your monster can be named whatever you want him to be named or her or them. (00:17:56): And Bob's job... I like to think his job is basically to make me the worst version of myself. He's the one that's like, oh, that person took all the fun Legos and you should go push them over and grab them back. Bob's job is... Bob's the one that wants to send the rage emails at 9:00PM and burn the house down. And the thing to learn about Bob is that, like I said, Bob never goes away. Bob is someone that you have to learn to deal with. But Bob's job is to make you the worst version of yourself. So your job is to let Bob do his thing, but not act on the emotions. Basically, all these emotions are normal and they are not useful. They are not the compass that should be telling you what to do. (00:18:46): But the other rule I have for managing Bob is a lot of people are like, oh, you're feeling off or tired or whatever. Go to bed and wake up tomorrow morning and you'll feel better. And the truth is that you're like, I want to send the rage email at 9:00PM. You still want to send it at 8:00AM. And a lot of these emotions just do not go away in 24 hours. So my rule of thumb from Facebook was give it two weeks. And the emotional, the sort of Bob... Bob is like these waves and they just roll through. So you made a new hire or somebody came in or you got layered or whatever. You'll have a set of reactions. And those reactions, again, they're normal, but they're not useful. They're not the ones that you should listen to. They are Bob. (00:19:29): And typically they go away in a couple of days, you get something new. Some new wave. But anything that lasts longer than two weeks is actually something you should pay attention to. It's something that if it's been around for two weeks, it's something you should go talk to someone about. Whether it's a manager or a friend or a coach or someone like that. That's the real stuff. Everything else is just Bob.
turns.zh: 正如我所说，我的脑子总爱用些奇怪的比喻。这真是个奇怪的大脑。我是在《布偶秀》的陪伴下长大的，我觉得这种情绪过山车般的体验——伴随成长、变革而来的情绪起伏——源自童年时期对奇奇怪怪动物的观察。不过说真的，我在某个时刻意识到，伴随晋升、成长和任何变革而来的情绪风暴，永远不会消失。无论你变得多么优秀……有时我甚至觉得，职位越高，这种情绪反而越强烈。因为你总觉得自己应该掌控全局，结果却遭遇一个恶魔的攻击：谁TM当初请你来这儿的？所以我把这些与变革相关的情绪外化成一个小怪兽。我给我的怪兽取名叫鲍勃。你的怪兽可以随心所欲地命名。（00:17:56）鲍勃的职责……我觉得他的任务就是把我变得最糟糕。他会说：哦，那个人拿走了所有好玩的乐高积木，你应该去把它们推倒抢回来。鲍勃的职责是……鲍勃想在晚上9点发愤怒邮件，烧毁整栋房子。关键是，要明白鲍勃永远不会消失。你必须学会与他共处。但他的任务就是把你变得最糟糕。所以你的任务就是让鲍勃随心所欲，但不要被情绪左右。基本上，所有这些情绪都是正常的，但毫无用处。它们不是该指引你行动的指南针。（00:18:46）管理鲍勃的另一个秘诀是：很多人会说，哦，你情绪低落、疲惫之类的。睡一觉明天就好了。但事实是，你想在晚上9点发愤怒邮件。到了早上8点你还是想发。很多情绪不会在24小时内消失。所以我从Facebook那里学到一个经验法则：给它两周时间。情绪的波动就像波浪，会自然消退。比如新员工加入、被裁员之类的。你会有各种反应。这些反应正常，但没用。它们是鲍勃的把戏。（00:19:29）通常几天后就会消失，迎来新波浪。但持续两周以上的情绪才是值得关注的。如果你持续两周，就该找人倾诉了。无论是经理、朋友、教练之类的。这才是关键，其他都是鲍勃的把戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a rule of thumb for when it actually, when you shouldn't give away your Legos? When it's like, okay, maybe you should fight back on this layering or whatever.
turns.zh: 有没有经验法则，什么时候你真的不该把乐高积木让出去？比如，当你想反击裁员之类的情况时。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: No rule of thumb. In general, I would actually say embracing change is far better than fighting it. And almost invariably, you cannot see what is around the corner, but it is almost always the thing to focus on. A lot of times I think inside of change, we get focused on the past, and one of the most valuable things you can do as a manager and a leader is help people focus on the future. I think... I'm sure there are times when people have done it and regretted it and it has led them somewhere. (00:20:42): I think being layered, for example, is one of the hardest things for people inside these experiences where someone brings in a manager above you. And I've also seen so many stories of that ending up being a great thing for someone. Even though they couldn't see it at the time. So in general, I would just say, step into the future and let the past go and see what you're going to learn. And sometimes you'll learn that it's time to leave or that this isn't the right pile of Legos for you. But it'll end up taking you somewhere that's worth exploring. Holding onto things almost always leads us to the worst version of ourselves.
turns.zh: 没有什么固定的经验法则。总的来说，我认为拥抱变化远比抗拒变化要好得多。而你几乎总看不到即将到来的转机，但这往往才是你应当专注的方向。很多时候，我发现身处变革中的人们往往执着于过去，而作为管理者和领导者，最有价值的工作之一就是帮助人们专注于未来。我觉得……我确信有过人们这样做却追悔莫及，最终却因此迎来转机的时候。（00:20:42）比如，层级重叠往往是人们在这种经历中最难应对的挑战——当有人引入一位高于你的管理者时。我也见过许多因此迎来转机的人的故事。即便当时他们看不清局势，但最终的结果往往值得探索。紧抓不放往往会把我们引向最糟糕的自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a very Buddhist way of thinking too. Just don't cling.
turns.zh: 这也是一种佛系思维方式。别执着。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And I think another part of this metaphor, I don't know if you think of it this way. Is the Legos aren't even your Legos, right? They're like the CEO's Legos, the shareholders' Legos. So you think they're your Legos, but no, you're not in charge.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这个比喻还有另一层含义，不知道你有没有这样想过。乐高积木根本不是你的，对吧？它们是CEO的乐高积木，是股东的乐高积木。你以为那是你的乐高积木，但其实你没权力做主。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Well, it is... I will say one of the hard-earned things is it can feel very emotional and it can feel very personal. It can feel like your work... I don't know, it can feel like your life is on the line sometimes. Just your work life. Oh, gosh, this matters so much. And one of the things that you learn as you get more senior and just have seen stuff is it's going to be okay. A friend of mine says, careers are long and nobody tells you that. But they're long. And this moment feels so dire and it feels so hard and it feels scary and it's going to be okay. So yeah, it is hard to know in the moment. And I think the story is going to be long and this is going to be one chapter or maybe even a part of a chapter, not a whole chapter. So embrace the length.
turns.zh: 嗯，确实……我要说一个来之不易的领悟：这可能会让人情绪激动，也会让人感觉事关个人尊严。有时你会觉得自己的工作……我不知道，有时你会觉得自己的生活危在旦夕。只是工作生活而已。天啊，这事太重要了。随着职位晋升，你会发现这只是冰山一角。这只是人生旅程中的一章，甚至可能只是一部分章节，而不是整个篇章。所以，坦然接受这漫长的旅程吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To build on that point, I've realized this is my fourth career doing what I do now. Whatever the hell this is. I was a engineer and then I was a founder. Then I was a product manager, and then what the hell I do now. Whatever this is, that's a whole different path.
turns.zh: 再延伸一下这个观点，我意识到这是我第四次从事现在所做的职业了。无论这到底算什么。我曾是工程师，然后是创始人，接着是产品经理，再到现在做什么鬼知道的工作。无论这算什么，那都是完全不同的路径。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: You don't have a name for it yet, Lenny?
turns.zh: 你还没给它起个名字吗，莱尼？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't. I hate all the terms people use for this world.
turns.zh: 没有。我讨厌人们用来形容这个世界的所有术语。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Somebody called me an influencer and I almost ripped their face off.
turns.zh: 有人叫我“网红”，我差点把他撕了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. [inaudible 00:23:02].
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: [inaudible 00:23:02].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, man. The most interesting careers are winding and they have starts and stops and failures and successes and control. Anybody that's been through a lot of this stuff, control is usually not the name of the game. It's usually just like, "Let's see what happens. We're going to try this and we're going to see what happens next."
turns.zh: 是啊，伙计。最有趣的职业生涯往往曲折坎坷，充满起起落落、挫折与成功、以及对局势的把控。任何经历过诸多波折的人都会明白，所谓"掌控全局"往往并非关键所在。更多时候，他们只会想："看看会发生什么吧。我们先试试看，再观察后续发展。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a great segue to another framework that I've heard from folks you've worked with that have been really impactful on them. So, Sarah Caldwell, who's a big deal at OpenAI, she told me that the framework that helped her most in her career is something that you call the J-Curve versus Stairs career growth framework. Talk about what that's about.
turns.zh: 接下来，我想顺便提一下另一个框架。这框架来自你共事过的一些人，对他们影响深远。比如，OpenAI 的萨拉·考德威尔（Sarah Caldwell）就告诉我，她职业生涯中受益最多的框架，是你提到的"J曲线与阶梯式职业发展"模型。能讲讲这个模型的核心内容吗？

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I actually gave a TED Talk about this one a couple of years ago because I am so passionate about it, but you can listen to the very packaged eight-minute version of this, but I will tell you the real story because it's very relevant to a lot of folks that listen to your podcast. I was at Facebook for five years. Like I said, the first two years I was in HR and I was doing employment branding and culture work and I was ready to stay there. I think I had in my head I was going to stay there until we went public, that was my plan just because I wanted to help the company through that moment, again, in my head. (00:24:21): This guy that many people know, Chamath Palihapitiya, came to me and Chamath ran growth and mobile at the time. And he came to me and we had lunch and he said in his very Chamath way, "You're useless. What are you doing in HR? This is stupid. You should come work for me." And anybody that knows Chamath is like, "Yes, that is actually what he said." He managed to insult you and compliment you in one sentence. (00:24:47): He gave me all these options on his team. And then the last one he said to me was like, "I'm going to go build a mobile phone. Do you want to come do that with me?" And I had four simultaneous reactions. The first was like, " That is incredibly stupid. Why are we doing that?" And then it was like, "Is that actually a thing that we're doing?" And then it was like, "Whoa, I think that sounds kind of fun." And so I left the conversation at Chamath and I went and asked my boss, Lori Goler, who's the head of people at Facebook for a very long time, like, "Is this actually something we're doing?" And she was like, "I can't believe he offered you that, whatever." (00:25:21): And I basically just could not get it out of my head, but it didn't make any sense, A, that Chamath had asked me because I was in HR. Like, "What am I doing? I don't absolutely jack shit about mobile." But I had worked on a project with him and I guess he thought I was smart. And I talked to Cheryl and she was like, "Well, that project will be dead in two months, but you can do it because you'll still have a job here." My dad was like, "Well, don't do that. " And anyway, a lot of very wise people being like, "Don't do that." (00:25:51): But I kind of couldn't get out of my head. And my friend said to me, "You've proven you're really good at this sort of company-wide project management and HR. Why don't you go show yourself how actually good you are? Is this transferable?" So, I took the job and I spent the next six months feeling like an absolute idiot. I basically felt like a total jackass all the time. I was sitting in rooms with these brilliant people asking the dumbest questions of my life and at the end of the six months, Chamath, I think, took a lot of pride in giving me the lowest performance rating I've ever gotten in my life, and it just felt like falling off a cliff. Then, slowly, I remember I had been doing all these trips to Taiwan because we were actually working on hardware and I, at some point, came back from Taiwan and I drew on a whiteboard for him the layout of a mobile phone and trying to explain to him why something he wanted to do was not possible. I so vividly remember walking out of that meeting being like, "Oh, I actually know things." And slowly then, over the following three years, I became an expert in mobile. And I basically... The phone itself was a giant failure, massive, costly failure for Facebook, but it was not a failure for me. It was a huge job that taught me that I was capable of things that I never could have dreamed of if I had stayed in HR. It set me up to be capable of taking on things that I didn't know about. (00:27:28): Chamath, when he pitched me on this job, actually drew me a picture on a whiteboard. He said, "Look, you can stay..." The way a lot of people do careers is a set of stairs. "You can be boring." To use Chamath, "And stay on these stairs. Just walk up the stairs and you'll get promoted every two years and your title will change from manager to senior manager to director to senior director, whatever." And he was like, "But that is boring." And he's like, "The much more fun careers are like jumping off cliffs." Basically, that you jump off this thing and you do fall for a period of time. I always like to say it's about six to nine months, but then this thing happens where you climb out. (00:28:05): And the picture he drew had this J-curve sort of basically leading you to places that are way beyond where the stairs could ever get you. And to be totally honest, that has been my experience. That taking risks, accepting the sort of terrible fall and that experience of falling has been more than worth it. Part of the reason why Sarah mentions it is that I do give this sort of talk to people that are inside of really fast-growing companies, because it's such an important place to let go of Legos and jump off cliffs because there's so much opportunity. And it is a place where if you prove to people that you're actually good, if they believe that you are the kind of person that they can use to do lots of things, you can get these opportunities that you are just so deeply unqualified for, but they can take you to places that you could never have imagined. (00:29:01): You can come out of those companies with skills that no one would ever have reasonably hired you to do. But I ended my time at Facebook in product and did business development and hardware and a whole bunch of the stuff along the way. And again, nobody would've hired me to do that at the beginning, but it's just because I kept saying yes to things.
turns.zh:
实际上，我几年前就曾在TED大会上谈论过这个话题，因为我对此充满热情。不过你们可以听听那个经过精心剪辑的八分钟版本，但我还是想跟你们分享真实的故事，因为这对很多听你播客的人都非常有意义。我在Facebook工作了五年。正如我所说，我最初的两年在人力资源部门，从事招聘品牌和企业文化方面的工作，本打算一直待在那里。我记得当时计划一直待到公司上市，因为我想帮助公司度过那个关键时期。（00:24:21）：Facebook的增长部门负责人查马斯·帕利哈皮蒂亚（Chamath Palihapitiya）找过我。他当时在Facebook负责增长和移动业务。他约我共进午餐，用他特有的直率方式说：“你太没用了。你干嘛在人力资源部？这太蠢了。你应该来为我工作。”熟悉查马斯的人都知道，他就是能用一句话既侮辱你又夸赞你的人。（00:24:47）：他向我提供了团队里的多个职位，最后问：“我要去开发手机产品，你想加入吗？”我当时有四种反应。第一种是：“这太蠢了。我们为啥要做这个？”第二种是：“我们真有这个项目？”第三种是：“哇，这听起来还挺有趣的。”于是我离开查马斯的办公室，找Facebook人力资源部主管洛丽·戈勒（Lori Goler）确认：“我们真有这个项目吗？”她回答：“真不敢相信他会邀请你，不过无所谓啦。” （00:25:21）：这个提议在我脑海里挥之不去，但根本说不通。首先，查马斯邀请我是因为我在人力资源部。再者，我对移动业务一窍不通。但我之前和他合作过一个项目，他可能觉得我挺聪明的。我找了谢丽尔（Cheryl），她说：“那个项目两个月后就会夭折，但你能胜任，因为你还能留在Facebook。”我爸说：“别去。”总之，许多明智之士都劝我别去。 （00:25:51）：但我始终念念不忘。朋友说：“你证明了自己很擅长公司级项目管理和人力资源工作。何不去证明一下自己的价值？这技能可迁移啊。” 于是我接受了这份工作，接下来六个月感觉自己像个十足的白痴。每次开会，我都坐在一群天才面前，问出自己这辈子最蠢的问题。六个月后，查马斯给了我生涯最低绩效评级，感觉坠入深渊。后来，我常去台湾出差参与硬件项目，某次回来后在白板上画手机设计图，试图解释他的构想不可行。这次会议后，我清晰记得走出会议室时想：“哦，我还真懂不少。” 接下来的三年，我逐渐成为移动领域专家。最终……这款手机对Facebook来说是惨痛失败，但对我而言却是一次重大突破。这份工作教会我，我比自己想象的更有能力。
假如我留在人力资源部门，我本可以梦想得到的东西。但这份工作让我有能力去挑战那些我一无所知的领域。（00:27:28）：查马特向我推荐这份工作时，还在白板上给我画了一幅图。他说：“看，你可以一直待在……” 很多人规划职业生涯时，把它比作一座阶梯。“你可以选择平庸的路径。”用查马特的话说：“一直沿着这座阶梯往上爬，每两年升职一次，头衔从经理到高级经理，再到总监，直至高级总监。” 但他反驳道：“那样太无聊了。” 他说：“更有趣的职业生涯就像从悬崖上跳下。”基本上，跳下悬崖后你会经历一段跌落期。我常说这个过程需要6到9个月，但随后你总能爬起来。
（00:28:05）：他画的图像是一条J型曲线，引领你到达阶梯永远无法触及的境界。说实话，这就是我的亲身经历。承担风险、接受那种惨烈的跌落，经历这种过程绝对是值得的。莎拉提起这段经历的部分原因，是我常向快速发展的公司内部人士分享这种观点。因为在这样的环境中，放下条条框框、勇敢跳下悬崖尤为重要，因为机会实在太过丰厚。只要你能证明自己的价值，证明自己是能胜任多项任务的人，你就能获得超出自己现有资质的机会，这些机会会带你到达意想不到的高度。
（00:29:01）：你能从这些公司走出来，掌握那些原本根本不会有人聘用你去做的技能。但我在Facebook的最后阶段，跨越了多个领域——产品开发、商业拓展、硬件研发等等。同样，一开始没人会雇我做这些工作，但正因为我不断勇于尝试，最终收获了超出预期的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Molly, I got tingles listening to this story. Wow.
turns.zh: 莫莉，听这个故事让我起了一身鸡皮疙瘩。哇哦。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Does it sound familiar, Lenny?
turns.zh: 莱尼，这听起来很熟悉吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It does. I want to ask, jumping off a cliff, sometimes you fall, really fall and you keep falling. Are there any kind of traits of like, "Okay, this is one that might be a J-Curve and worth the risk of falling, and this is when you should probably just not, let's not do this".
turns.zh: 确实。我想问一下，比如跳下悬崖，有时你会掉下去，真的掉下去，而且一直掉。是否有某种特质，比如，“好吧，这可能是J曲线风险，值得冒险掉下去”，而“这时候你或许就不该冒险，还是别这么做”。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah. I just think there are different kinds of fear. We talk a lot about this in Glue Club because one of the thing, there is a financial fear, right? Leaving a job and taking a job that has financial risk associated with it, or leaving a job and taking time off, which is something that I spend a lot of time talking to people about, you got to do the math and you got to... Sometimes there is a type of fear that is telling you like, "This is not the right time." Or, "I don't want to be financially anxious for months and months and months." (00:30:21): I use finances because it's the most concrete example of a type of fear that you should actually listen to. And sometimes you can do the math. I always counsel people through that. I'm like, "What is the number that you need to hit so that you're not constantly terrified financially?" And that number is wildly different for people based on their background and their life. "Can you do that? Can you consult, can you whatever in order to take this leap?" But a lot of times fear is just you saying, "I'm scared I can't do this. I'm scared I'm not capable of it. Yeah, I'm scared I'll fail." (00:30:56): And that's the kind of fear that I think of as a flashing green light because... And it sounds like Matt McGinnis said this too, where it's like, "That's the kind of fear that's saying, 'Why don't you go prove to yourself that you are actually capable of this?'" Or if you fail, like, "You'll have learned something, too." You know what I mean? You'll have learned, like, "I took this job in product at Facebook as my last chapter there, and let me tell you things that people should never fucking hire me to do." I was like, "I am not a good product manager." But I've got a great product mindset. I can sit in a bunch of chairs and hang with the product folks, but I'm not the person that cares about the button. Do you know what I mean? (00:31:38): And I would never have learned that. I wouldn't have known who I was if I hadn't taken that risk and failed or at least learned that it's not something I wanted to do again. So, there's many different lessons that come from facing down those fears and jumping off the cliff, but mostly what it is is knowing yourself better and knowing where you go next from there.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得恐惧有不同种类。我们在Glue Club里经常讨论这个，因为其中一个是财务恐惧，对吧？比如离职去承担财务风险，或者休假，这些都是我常和人们探讨的。你得算算账，得……有时候某种恐惧会告诉你，“现在不是时候。”或者，“我不想几个月几个月地财务焦虑下去。”（00:30:21）：我用财务例子是因为这是最具体的恐惧类型，你应该听从的。而有时你能算出那个数字。我总是这样劝别人：“你需要达到什么数字才能不再财务焦虑？”但这个数字因背景和生活不同而大相径庭。“你能做到吗？你能做咨询、做其他事来实现这个跨越吗？”但很多时候恐惧只是你说，“我害怕做不到。我害怕自己不行。”（00:30:56）：这种恐惧在我看来像绿灯闪烁，因为……马特·麦金尼斯也说过：“这种恐惧在说，‘你为什么不去证明自己真的能做到呢？’”或者如果你失败了，“你也会学到东西的。”懂我的意思吗？你会学到，比如，“我在Facebook的最后一个产品职位，让我告诉你，人们永远不该雇我做这些事。”我当时想，“我不是个好的产品经理。”但我有很棒的产品思维。我能坐在各种会议椅上，和产品团队打成一片，但我不在乎按钮的事。你懂我的意思吗？（00:31:38）：从面对这些恐惧、跳下悬崖中能收获很多不同的经验，但最重要的是更了解自己，知道下一步该往哪儿走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such helpful advice. I also love how you frame this of, "Prove it to yourself that you can do this." It's not, "I'm going to show them that I can do this." Because the way you describe this, usually it's an opportunity given to you. "Hey, can you do this thing? We want you to lead this new thing." And the fear is like, "I don't think I can do that." And what you're saying here is, "Prove it to yourself that you can." Or, I guess, it's also, "Okay, maybe I can't and then I'll learn that and then I'll know more about myself."
turns.zh: 这真是很有用的建议。我也喜欢你把它框定为“向自己证明你能做到”，而不是“我要向他们证明我能做到”。因为你描述的方式通常是别人给你的机会。“嘿，你能做这件事吗？我们想让你领导这个新项目。”而恐惧会说，“我觉得我做不到。”而你在这里说的是，“向自己证明你能做到。”或者，我猜，还有，“好吧，也许我做不到，那我就从中学到教训，然后更了解自己了。”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I mean, one of the greatest gifts in a career is knowing yourself. And that's a lifelong journey because who you are and what you want changes, but that knowledge and that gift, nothing accelerates your self-knowledge faster than trying to do something that you don't know how to do and that you're scared of.
turns.zh: 是啊，说得太对了。我觉得职业生涯中最珍贵的礼物之一，就是认识自己。这是一生的修行，因为你究竟是谁、你想要什么都会随时间变化，但这种认知和天赋——没有什么比尝试做你不会做且心怀恐惧的事，更能加速自我认知了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Probably the quote I use most on this podcast comes up again in my mind as you talk about this, this line that, "The cave you fear contains the treasure you seek."
turns.zh: 在你谈论这个话题时，我脑海中又浮现出我最常引用的名言：“你害怕的洞穴，里面藏着你追寻的宝藏。”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Hell yes, exactly. Well said.
turns.zh: 太对了，说得太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There it is.
turns.zh: 就是这样。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I haven't heard that one from you, so clearly I need to listen more.
turns.zh: 我还没听过你说这句话，看来我需要多听听你的分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that's great. I'm glad I don't overuse it. It just feels like it comes up again and again, and I think your point about the runway and the finances is such an important one because that's a very real practical question. One thing I did when I took time off, I took a year off after I left my job. What helped me was I just created a runway goal for myself. I'm just like, "Okay, here's what it's going to cost me for six months or a year to live without any income. Am I comfortable just burning through these tens of thousands of dollars to explore and see something new emerge?" And so you just have to feel good. "Okay, yes, I'm going to burn all that money and that's part of it."
turns.zh: 好的，很棒。我很高兴自己没有过度引用它。只是感觉这句话反复出现，我觉得你关于过渡期和财务的观点很重要，因为这是一个非常现实的实际问题。当我休假时，我离职后休息了一年。对我有帮助的是，我为自己设定了一个过渡目标。我就想：“好的，如果六个月或一年没有收入，我的生活成本是多少？我能安心地花掉这几万美元去探索和等待新机遇出现吗？”所以你必须感觉良好。“好的，没错，我要花掉这些钱，这也是过程的一部分。”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, that's exactly the exercise. You're saying "runway" I say "burn rate", so we both were raised inside of companies, incentive tech, but I think it is do the math, right? What can you afford? And it's both what can you afford and still feel safe? Because sometimes, I mean, again, I think that is different for everyone, but it is such an important set of math to do because, A, a lot of times that number is smaller than you think it is, then your brain makes it out to be if you have this sort of existential financial anxiety versus, I always say, "Specific financial anxiety is much more useful than existential financial anxiety." And some friends are leaving jobs and I'll be like, "Hey, your number is 5K or 10K a month. You have to believe that you can get a consulting gig that will pay you that. Do you believe that?" And it's like, "Either yes or no." And then, "Okay, either we're doing it or we're not.
turns.zh: 是啊，这正是关键所在。你说“过渡期”，我说“消耗率”，所以我们都在公司里待过，在激励技术领域工作过，但我认为关键在于计算成本，对吧？你能承受多少？同时还要确保心理安全感。这有时因人而异，但计算成本非常重要。首先，这个数字往往比你想象的要低，然后当你陷入存在主义财务焦虑时，大脑会放大问题。但我总说：“具体的财务焦虑比存在主义财务焦虑更有用。”有些朋友离职后，我会问：“嘿，你每月的开支是5000或10000美元。你得相信自己能找到一份能支付这个数额的咨询工作。你相信吗？” 他们要么说“是”，要么说“不是”。然后说：“好的，那我们要么行动，要么放弃。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other part of this J- Curve that I think is really important to touch on is this idea of for the first six or nine months, you're going to be at the bottom of the J curve falling, still falling. And some projects don't last that long and then you're like, "Okay, total failure. I never emerged from this fall." So, is there any advice there? Just, how do you create that enough space to give you a chance to start to un-fall?
turns.zh: J曲线中另一个我认为非常重要的部分是，前六到九个月，你会处于J曲线的底部，不断下滑。有些项目持续不了那么久，然后你会说：“好吧，总失败了。我从这场下滑中从未走出来。”那么，有什么建议吗？就是如何创造足够的空间，让你有机会开始不再下滑？

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I mean, the most valuable thing that happens as you fall is learning. And even on the other side of failure, you've learned a shit ton. I always say, "The most important thing to do in the falling phase and the risk taking land is to learn to embrace being a professional idiot." Basically, being the one that shows up at the meeting and is like, "What are we talking about? What does that word mean?" (00:35:18): For a bunch of reasons. Number one, you can learn so much. And again, even in the face of failure, no one can take away your learning. Do you know what I mean? But the other thing is that it turns out that a lot of the questions in the world that, you're sitting in the meeting and you're like, "This is a dumb question. Everyone's going to think I'm an idiot." But then you get brave and you ask it and it turns out it wasn't a dumb question. Do you know what I mean? Turns out that everyone had that question in their mind, but no one was brave enough to ask it. (00:35:48): So, from a skills' perspective, again, regardless of outcome, being the person that sort of takes their learning in their own hands, learning no matter what and learning to ask those dumb questions, it's a superpower. I always say that, "Actually, my superpower is being a professional moron." Because I'm the one that shows up in a room and is like, "Do we have goals? What are we doing? Why are we talking about this? Why are we having this meeting?" And most of the time it's actually what I was hired to do, which is bring clarity.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，当你经历失败时，最宝贵的收获就是学习。即便面对失败的结果，你也学到了无数东西。我常说：“在面临挑战和承担风险的阶段，最重要的是学会坦然接受自己是个‘专业白痴’的身份。”说白了，就是在会议上发言时问出“我们在聊什么？那个词什么意思？”这样看似傻乎乎的问题。（00:35:18）原因有很多。首先，你能从中收获大量经验。即便遭遇失败，也没人能剥夺你的学习机会。懂我的意思吧？另外很多时候，会议上你提出的那些看似愚蠢的问题，明明每个人心里都有疑惑，却没人有勇气开口。（00:35:48）所以从技能角度看，抛开结果不谈，主动掌握学习进程、坚持不懈提问那些看似愚蠢的问题，这本身就是一项超能力。我常说：“其实我的超能力就是当个‘专业白痴’。”因为我总是在会议上发问：“我们有目标吗？在做什么？为什么讨论这个？开这个会的意义何在？”而大多数时候，这些问题恰恰是我被雇来解决的——让事情清晰明了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny. I just recorded a podcast episode with a PM named Zevi who joined Wix and he had this thought, he's like a very young PM, just getting started and he's like, "Okay, I need to be a 10X PM because that's what they expect of me, that's what everyone that is really good, that's how I think of a 10X PM." And then he went into his first meeting and he just failed and he just felt so bad. He's like, "I guess I'm not that 10X PM. They're all going to see that. They think I'm terrible." And then he did another presentation a little bit later and people were so impressed with how he learned and evolved and improved. And he realized that he needs to be not a 10X PM, but a 10X learner, and that's what people actually expect from someone, especially a junior person.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我刚和Wix的一位产品经理Zevi录制了一期播客。他初入职场，刚接触PM岗位，就想：“我得成为10倍效率的产品经理，毕竟大家都期望如此。”结果参加第一场会议就翻车了，感觉糟透了。他说：“看来我根本不是10倍效率的产品经理，大家肯定觉得我太差劲了。” 但后来他再做演示时，大家对他的学习能力和进步印象深刻。这时他才意识到，关键不在于成为10倍效率的产品经理，而是要成为10倍效率的学习者——这才是人们真正期待的，尤其是对初级从业者而言。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I was having a conversation last night with a friend of mine who has a senior in high school and I was like, "What is the plan? What are we telling this senior in high school to think about relative to their career given everything that's going on with AI?" And we talked about it a bunch, but what we both circled back to was this idea of soft skills and that actually the only thing you can really anchor on right now is that teaching kids grit, teaching them hard work, teaching them learning, right? Learning how to learn, loving learning, being able to fall, in a world that's changing this fast. And I say this inside of companies too, right? I always say, like, "What you know today is way less valuable than what you can learn by tomorrow." If you're inside of a company where the growth curve is like this, what you know today is irrelevant. (00:37:52): Somebody once told... I'm sure this is faster now, but they rewrote the entire code base at Google every eight years, which means that if you're not learning, if you're not evolving, then you become irrelevant and extinct. So, setting the goal by itself, not enough, you have to build a process in the system to actually learn from the goal.

是啊，我完全同意。我觉得公司设定的目标不应该超过六个，但现实就是这样。首先，我想从高层视角谈两点，再具体展开目标设定的思路。一是关于OKR（目标与关键结果）的争议。我觉得它对谷歌等公司确实很有用，但很多时候，当我进入一家公司，或者和高管交流时问“你们的目标是什么”，得到的往往是一份长达100行的电子表格，内容复杂得让人看得头疼。这时候我就会想：“这根本无法清晰传达目标。”归根结底，目标的意义在于沟通——它们本质上就是一种沟通工具，旨在明确方向，帮助员工明确日常工作重点。但那种100行表格根本起不到这个作用。

（00:48:23）第二点是，公司需要根据自身阶段调整策略。种子期公司和成熟企业对目标的需求截然不同。比如我在种子期公司时，每两个月就会迭代设定目标；而成熟企业可能更适合年度目标。但年度目标对早期公司来说往往是浪费时间。

（00:48:58）我从Facebook学到很多经验，他们在这方面做得很好。Facebook在我任职的五年里始终坚持三个公司目标：增长（以月活用户数为衡量指标）、用户参与度（衡量用户回访频率）和营收。这三个目标足以管理整个公司。任何公司都不需要超过三个目标。

（00:49:52）第三点是，目标必须有明确的主导项。比如，当我需要分配当天的工作重点时，必须明确最重要的任务。在Facebook，增长目标是核心，但增长数据有两种计算方式：一是购买印尼僵尸粉来虚增MAU；二是提升用户参与度。这让我深刻认识到，参与度才是核心指标。只有专注于提升参与度，才能真正驱动营收增长，成就核心业务价值。

（00:50:35）最后一点是目标的可理解性。目标必须像五岁小孩都能听懂的简单指南。新入职的实习生应该能清晰理解目标内容，否则说明沟通失败了。目标必须明确易懂，易于执行。
解释这些缩写时，必须使用普通人能理解的数字，否则它就无法作为有效的沟通工具。（00:51:03）：第四个要点是……实际上，我借用了克莱尔·休斯·约翰逊（Claire Hughes Johnson）的一个说法。她曾做客你的播客，还写了一本名为《Scaling People》的书。她说了一句话，我很喜欢——“策略应该带来痛苦”。我过去的角色是设定非目标，基本上就是把你不打算做的事和打算做的事说清楚，但“策略应该带来痛苦”这种说法能更好地向人们解释这个概念。如果你不做出痛苦的取舍，就无法帮助人们优先分配时间。因为工作的本质是人们每天都会出现，完成一些任务。要么你明确告知他们优先事项是什么，要么他们会自行决定每天的工作重点。我们在创业者身上经常看到这种情况，他们无法从清单上删减任务，就坚持设定10个目标。我会说：“很好。其中6个目标根本无法完成，所以要么你自己决定选哪4个，要么别人会替你决定。” 所以，策略应该带来痛苦。如果你的目标设定过程没有痛苦，那就说明你对优先级的重视程度不够。

（00:52:09）：好的，准备好了吗？我们来讲第五个要点。虽然这更多是组织层面的问题，但对水线模型也很重要，那就是每个目标都有一个负责人。你设定了一个数字，旁边写着负责人的名字。如果你无法完成这项工作，那就说明你没有做最重要的工作来确保这些目标得以实现。这是组织层面的工作，非常痛苦，因为有时人们会想，哦，这个或那个可以负责，或许他们会一起负责，但两个人的目标等于没有负责。一个目标，一个负责人。最后也是最难的一点是，仅靠目标是不够的。我和很多创业者交流过，他们会说：“我做到了。我设定了目标。为什么没效果？我不明白。” 我会问：“设定目标后你做了什么？” 他们会说：“我不知道，我就设定了目标。” 目标……（00:53:10）：詹姆斯·克利尔（James Clear）在《原子习惯》中写了一句很棒的话：赢家和输家有相同的目标。仅靠目标是不够的，你还需要有一个流程来跟进目标，监督人们对目标负责，并从目标中学习。因为在目标设定方面，尤其是在公司早期阶段，大多是在从尝试做某事中学习。你设定一个目标，我们能做到吗？移动这个数字有多难？这才是……你可能会一直犯错，但你正在学习如何移动这个数字。所以，仅设定目标是不够的，你必须在系统中建立一个流程来真正从目标中学习。

turns.en: Wow. This list is ... There's so much power in this list, it's such a succinct-
turns.zh: 哇。这份清单……里面蕴含着巨大的能量，简洁明了——

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: It's too long.
turns.zh: 太长了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I don't think it is because each of these has so much depth and power to them that saves you so much headache and just wasted time and resources. I don't know. You just don't care as much about hitting that goal. And if it's you-
turns.zh: 不，我不这么认为，因为每一条都蕴含着深刻的洞见和强大力量，能为你节省大量精力和资源，避免浪费时间和资源。就拿“一个老板、一个目标”这个理念来说，我个人深有体会，因为如果你觉得别人可能在做这件事，或者觉得这不是你的全责，那么你的精力和专注度就会大打折扣。你根本不会那么在意达成目标。而如果是你的话——

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, accountability.
turns.zh: 对，就是责任追究制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. If it's like, "Lenny, this goal is your goal and, if you hit it, you've done it. If you don't, you've done a bad job," that'd be a such motivating, so motivating. If it's me and Molly, okay, well, we'll figure it out.
turns.zh: 没错。比如说，“莱尼，这个目标就是你的目标，达成了，就是你的功劳；达不成，就是你做得不行。”这种激励方式太管用了。如果是莫莉和我，那好吧，我们再想办法解决。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: It creates a flood of clarity that seeps down from the person too. And to go back to the waterline model, I would say, so often you'll actually find companies that have set goals but no one owns the goals, everyone owns the goals, multiple people own the goal and you didn't actually get all the way to the answer. And I will say that the ownership thing is hard, it can feel painful but it's really important. There's only one owner and that means that that person, come hell or high water, owns that number.
turns.zh: 这会让清晰的思路从上而下渗透下来。回到水线模型，我想说，很多公司设定了目标，但没人真正负责。每个人都分担责任，结果却一事无成。说真的，责任追究制很难执行，可能会让人感到痛苦，但它真的很重要。只有一个人负责，无论如何都要达成目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The way I described it [inaudible 00:55:18] was just someone's ass has to be on the line for this and that just works. That's such a powerful lever to drive things to have one person responsible.
turns.zh: 对。我之前描述的[00:55:18的音频缺失]就是要让某个人为此负责，这样才有效。让一个人全权负责，就是推动事情进展的强大杠杆。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: The other's just this idea of strategy hurting, I love that. I love that phrase, I forgot Claire had that. So true.
turns.zh: 另一个观点是战略可能适得其反，我喜欢这个说法。忘了克莱尔说过这句话了，太对了。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: So good.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because the whole idea is you need to not do things, you need to decide what you're not ... The whole strategy, a big part of it is what we are not doing.
turns.zh: 整个理念就是你得摒弃一些事情，决定不做什么。整个战略的核心部分，就是我们不该做什么。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And if you're not making painful choices, then you're not actually doing it.
turns.zh: 对，绝对是这样。如果你不做出痛苦的选择，那你根本就没在真正行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this idea of three goals, so is it just ... So, do you go into a company and just go through a checklist essentially of here's the six things I look at to tell me where there's opportunity to improve?
turns.zh: 还有三个目标的这个理念，是不是就是……那你去一家公司，基本上就是用这份清单来检查，看看有没有可以改进的机会？

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: When I work with founders and I see their goals, I use it as a way to get to know the business and I'm just going to be literally like, "What is this? What are you trying to explain?" And I can usually, through asking a lot of really dumb questions which, like I said, one of my superpowers, get them to explain to me the one sentence and the one number that they're actually trying to get across but it takes work and that's part of ... It's almost easier to write the 100-line spreadsheet than it is to say, "Wait, what are the three drivers of this business genuinely? What are they and how do they relate to each other?" And there can be things underneath them but there's three at the top that matter. So, yeah, I'm not a scientific person about it but a lot of it is just by asking people to explain their businesses to me, you can basically find the drivers.
turns.zh: 与创始人合作时，我会通过他们的目标来了解他们的业务。我通常会直截了当地问：“这是什么？你想解释什么？” 通过提出许多看似愚蠢的问题——正如我所说，这是我的专长之一——我通常能让他们解释清楚他们真正想传达的一句话和一个数字。但这需要努力，这也是……把写100行电子表格比起说"等等，这个业务的三个核心驱动因素是什么？它们是什么，又是如何相互关联的？"要容易得多。虽然表层可能有复杂的因素，但最重要的三个核心驱动力才是关键。所以，我不是个严谨的科学家，但通过让人们向我解释他们的业务，你基本上就能找到那些核心驱动力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the story about Facebook having these same three goals for five years, considering their success, you may think they're not as complicated as your business but I am confident they're just as, if not, more complicated. And to your point, if it's not hurting, then you're doing something wrong.
turns.zh: 还有关于Facebook五年来始终坚持同样的三个目标的故事。考虑到他们的成功，你可能会认为他们的业务不像你的那么复杂，但我确信它们同样复杂，甚至更复杂。他们是市场平台、社交网络、广告业务，内部情况错综复杂。但只要能围绕三个核心目标展开工作，你也能做到这一点。正如你所说，如果这没造成困扰，那你肯定做错了。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。
