Moving on to another topic, you have not necessarily rules but rules of thumb that you find really helpful for people to have in their head as they're dealing with change and scale and growth and all that kind of stuff so let's just walk through that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种方式……这正是我希望这次聊天能达到的效果，每个小片段都自成一体，完全可以单独做成播客，畅谈几个小时。所以我对目前的进展非常兴奋。接下来转到另一个话题。你没有固定的规则，但有些经验法则对人们应对变化、规模扩张和增长等挑战非常有帮助，让我们一起探讨一下。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah. So, for leaders that are leading through change and growth, the list is probably long but I always say to people don't come to me for management 101, I'm not the person to ask on how to run the most effective one-on-one with your people. What I think is not talked about enough is what it takes to manage and lead through change and that is a very particular set of feelings. And the first thing I learned, when someone makes you a manager or when you take a job as a leader inside a company, you really do feel like, "Oh, who gave me this job?" and you feel like you're supposed to know the answer to things. People come to you and ask questions and you're like, "I'm supposed to know. I'm a leader, I am supposed to have answers." (00:58:35): And I think, particularly inside of rapid change and scale and growth, it's really important to understand that your job as manager and a leader is not to have all the answers. It is not to have all the answers, it is to get good at finding them, it is to get good at bringing people together to find the answers. And that is hard because it requires saying, "I don't know, let's go figure it out," a whole bunch and it's scary as a leader to say I don't know because you think, "Oh, gosh, people are going to see through me." But again, the more you travel in life, the more you realize that the most experienced leaders are the ones that say, "No, no, no," all the time.
turns.zh: 是的。对于引领变革和增长的领导者来说，要遵循的清单可能很长，但我总是告诉人们别来找我讲管理基础课程，我不是教你如何与员工进行最高效一对一沟通的专家。我认为最被忽视的是如何管理和领导变革所需的心态。这是一套非常特殊的情感体验。我学到的第一个教训是，当有人让你当经理，或者你接手公司领导职位时，你真的会觉得"天哪，谁让我接手这个职位的？"你觉得自己应该对所有事情都了如指掌。人们来问你问题时，你会想"我应该知道答案。我是领导者，必须给出答案。" （00:58:35）：我认为，在快速变化、规模扩张和增长的环境中，重要的是要明白，管理者和领导者的职责不是知晓所有答案，而是要善于寻找答案，善于召集团队共同寻找答案。这很难，因为这需要不断说"我不知道，让我们一起找答案"，但作为领导者，这样做很吓人，因为你会觉得"天哪，人们会看穿我的虚伪。"但再一次，随着人生阅历的增加，你会发现最有经验的领导者总是不断说"不，不，不"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is a good reminder of this Bob the monster concept because, hearing this, okay, I don't need to have all the answers as a leader. In real life, being in a meeting, people are like, "Hey, Molly, what do you think of this?" You're like, "Oh, I should have a good answer." And so, I think that's a good reminder of this idea of this Bob the monster is going to tell you, "Oh, you don't know anything, you're not ready for this. You suck at this, you're going to fail everyone that's [inaudible 00:59:34]."
turns.zh: 我觉得这很好地提醒了我们“鲍勃怪兽”这个概念。听完这些话，我意识到，作为领导者，你不需要知晓所有答案。在现实生活中，开会时人们会问：“嘿，莫莉，你对此有什么看法？”你可能会想：“天啊，我应该有个好答案才对。” 所以，我认为这很好地提醒了我们，“鲍勃怪兽”会对你说：“哦，你什么都不懂，你还没准备好。你做得很烂，你会让所有人失望的……”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: They're regretting hiring you.
turns.zh: 他们后悔雇用了你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊，确实。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Everyone's going to see through you. Imposter, imposter, imposter.
turns.zh: 大家都会看穿你的。冒名顶替者，冒名顶替者，冒名顶替者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, 100%.
turns.zh: 没错，百分之百。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But just remembering, there's going to be this part of your head and that's okay, it's there but it doesn't mean it's true.
turns.zh: 但只要记住，你脑海中会有这样的声音，这没关系，它存在，但并不意味着它是真的。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Absolutely. And these things are muscles. Dealing with Bob as a muscle, learning to not react to all those things that attack you but also learning, oh, in this moment when someone asks me a question and I'm like, "Oh," actually I should be like, "I don't actually know, let's go ... Who should we ask? How can we learn this? How can we explore this together? What do you think?" Those are all actually very powerful questions and they're terrifying to, particularly earlier in your career, as a leader and a manager.
turns.zh: 绝对的。这些能力就像肌肉一样。把“鲍勃”当作肌肉来应对，学会不去回应那些攻击你的声音，同时也要学会，当有人问我问题时，我会说：“哦，”但实际上我应该说：“我其实也不知道，让我们……该找谁呢？我们怎么才能学到这些？我们一起探索一下好吗？” 这些都是非常有力的提问，但对于职业生涯早期的领导者和管理者来说，它们却令人心生恐惧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So, yeah, so the lesson there is no one expects you to have all the answers as a leader.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以，是的，关键在于，作为领导者，没人期望你知晓所有答案。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不会的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: And particularly in this world, the one that's changing as fast as it is, nobody knows. Nobody knows what the answers are in a lot of cases, the war will be won by the people that are good exploring and figuring it out.
turns.zh: 尤其是在这个变化如此迅速的世界里，很多时候没人知道答案。战争将由那些善于探索和解决问题的人赢得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that phrase.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个说法。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: So, the second one is, and everyone that has learned this has learned it the hard way, do not promise things that you can't control. It's so tempting particularly when you're hiring people to be like, "Oh, yeah, your onboarding will be smooth and calm and everything's clear and we've figured it ... Let us tell you our vision and how obvious and clear and smart and blah, blah, blah." And then they show up and it's like, "Oh, shit," you know what I mean? There's no manual, no one knows what they're doing, it's all ambiguity and chaos. It's so easy when someone says I want to know that I'm going to be your CMO forever to be like, "Sure, you can be my CMO," you don't know that. Do you know what I mean? So, being really careful with promises of things that are out of your control like stability or titles or never hiring over someone is a flashing red light because there is literally no faster way to demoralize high performers than going back on a promise. Everyone that has been through it knows that feeling of like, "They told me this when I joined," and then they don't do it and you're like, "Well, fuck this place." So, no faster way to demoralize people or to hire the wrong people than promising things that are actually out of your control. Being honest and upfront about who you are as a company, about what you're able to promise, all of that is actually ... It's very hard work but it's so important because so much is out of your control and you need to hire people that are cool with that.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来是第二个要点——每个学过这一课的人都是吃了苦头才明白的：别轻易许下无法兑现的承诺。这太诱人了，尤其是当你招人时会说：“哦，对，你的入职流程会很顺利、很顺畅，一切都清晰明了，我们已经规划好了……让我们来向你阐述我们的愿景吧，多么清晰明了、多么高明等等等等。” 但当新人到岗后，现实往往是：“哦，该死！” 你懂我的意思吧？根本没有操作手册，没有人知道该怎么做，到处都是模糊不清和混乱。当有人说“我要永远担任你的首席营销官”时，你就得小心应对——你根本无法保证这一点。你懂我的意思吧？所以，对稳定性、职位头衔、绝不招人等超出自己控制范围的事务做出承诺时，必须格外谨慎，因为食言最能打击高潜人才的士气。每个经历过这种挫折的人都知道那种感觉：“我入职时他们是这么说的，结果却食言了。” 然后你就会说：“去他的，这地方真操蛋。” 所以，许下超出自己控制范围的承诺，是最快打击员工士气、招错人的方法。诚实面对公司的真实情况、明确能兑现的承诺，所有这些努力都意义非凡——虽然过程艰难，但至关重要，因为太多事情超出你的掌控范围，而你需要招来能接受这一现实的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love that. I learned this the hard way once, I had a ... One of my early projects, we were late and the head of product was just so pissed he's like, "Because I've been telling the CEO it's going to be on time because you've been telling me it's going to be on time and then it wasn't and why didn't you tell me that?" And I was just like, "Okay, it'll never happen again," and he's like, "You can't ... Don't tell me that because that's not true, that nay not ... You can't guarantee that." And so, that taught me that lesson of just, yeah, you're right, you want to say that, it feels so good. Okay, this will never happen again but you can't and they know you can't promise things like that.
turns.zh: 太赞了。我也吃过这个苦头。有次我的一个早期项目延期了，产品负责人气急败坏地质问：“我一直跟CEO说项目会按时完成，而你也一直这么说结果却延期了，你为什么不告诉我？” 我只好说：“好吧，下次不会再这样了。” 他却说：“你不能……别这么说，那不真实，根本……你不能保证这些。” 这让我深刻领悟到，许下无法兑现的承诺，看似让人感觉良好，实则适得其反。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah. And sorry, I'm going to quote Claire Hughes Johnson again but she has this really fun phrase that she said in a talk at Glue Club that I've now latched onto and stolen from her which is, she was like, "Promises like that are like letter bombs that you mail yourself that are going to explode in your face in a year," and I was like, "That is the perfect metaphor." Because it's short-term pain, you want to make this person feel good right now so you promise them something but, in one year, you're going to make them feel terrible so don't do it.
turns.zh: 是啊。对不起，我又要引用克莱尔·休斯·约翰逊的话了。她在Glue Club的一次演讲中说了一句很棒的比喻：“这种承诺就像你寄给自己的炸弹信件，过一年就会炸到你自己脸上。” 我当时就觉得：“这比喻太贴切了。” 因为短期内你想让对方开心，就许下承诺，但一年后他们会后悔不已，所以千万别这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great advice. All right, keep going.
turns.zh: 好建议。继续吧。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah. So, again, could probably go on the topic of what it takes to manage and lead forever inside this stuff but I'll give you two more that I yell about a lot in Glue Club. The first is that we spend huge amounts of time talking about hiring. How do you get good at hiring? What's the right interview? How do I find the right people? Firing people is as important as hiring people. Getting good at identifying when someone does not belong or someone is not going to work out is actually a skill and being good at it as a company and as a leader is as important as identifying the right talent because, eventually, if you're not good at firing people, what you have is essentially barnacles on a ship. Really going forward with the ship metaphor, anyway.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以，再说一次，关于如何管理和领导团队的主题，我还能讲很久，但我再分享两个我在Glue Club里经常强调的观点吧。首先，我们花大量时间讨论招聘问题。如何成为招聘高手？正确的面试流程是什么？如何找到合适的人才？解雇员工和招聘人才同样重要。能够识别出不适合团队或无法胜任工作的人才，实际上是一项技能。作为公司和领导者，如果能掌握这项技能，其重要性不亚于识别出优秀人才。因为如果解雇员工的能力不行，团队最终就会像船上附着的藤壶一样，成为累赘。反正我还是想继续用船的比喻来打个比方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's true.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: It's drag people that are sitting around not pushing the team forward. So, it's painful and it's horrible because it is humans but, when someone doesn't fit, you ... No one is right all the time when it comes to hiring, I actually say most people are wrong half the time. The best people in the world in hiring will tell you they have about a 50% average in terms of being right. That means half the hires don't work out. That means, half the time, you're going to need to fire the person. So, it's such an important skill to get good at particularly when you're going through a lot of change. And the last one is humans are messy and it's very emotional. And when you're a leader, particularly if you have any kind of anagram too or just if you like to make people happy and you want to be liked, it can be so hard to lead teams because you get tangled in the people. Firing people is a painful experience, reorganizing things, layering people, all these things are emotionally painful for the people and they're emotionally painful for you as a manager. (01:05:05): But my mantra that almost always leads in the best direction is serve the business, not the people meaning everyone is better off if this company is wildly successful. Everyone looks smart and makes lots of money or whatever if this company grows and does what we all dream it can. So, at the end of the day, the best decisions, the ones that are always going to be right are the ones that are like, "How do we do the right thing for this business?" And it also helps in political situations. Someone's acting weird or their Bob is raging all over the company, technically, everyone has the same goal. The goal is to build the biggest business possible, that's the answer. The answer is always what's the right thing for the business. And the people stuff can fall away when you actually focus on what's the right thing for the business.
turns.zh: 那些消极拖后腿、不推动团队前进的人才是最难缠的。所以这很痛苦，也很令人头疼，因为这关乎人性。但当有人不合适时，你……说实话，大多数人在招聘决策上都常犯错误。我听说全球顶尖招聘专家，正确率平均只有50%。这意味着半数招聘失败，意味着半数时候你不得不解雇员工。因此，掌握这项技能至关重要，尤其是在公司经历重大变革时。最后一点是，人性是复杂且情绪化的。作为领导者，尤其是如果你有同理心或喜欢取悦他人时，领导团队会异常困难，因为你会深陷于员工的情感纠葛中。解雇员工是痛苦的经历，重组团队、调整人员结构……这些对员工和管理者来说都充满情感上的折磨。（01:05:05）：但我最常遵循的准则是——为业务服务，而非为人服务。这意味着只要公司成功，每个人都能受益。如果公司发展顺利，每个人都会看起来很聪明，赚大钱……所以归根结底，最明智的决策永远是问自己：“如何为公司做正确的事？”这在处理政治局面时也很有用。当有人行为怪异，或者他们的‘鲍勃’在公司里到处发脾气时，本质上，大家的目标是一致的——打造尽可能大的业务，这才是答案。答案永远是为业务做正确的事。当你真正专注于为业务做正确的事时，人事问题就会自然而然地消失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A really useful tool to do that that I learned from my manager is to think about, when you're trying to decide whether to fire someone or change a project even though it's going to upset someone, is to say, "Okay, if there were no emotions involved, if this person had no negative reaction to this, what would I do?"
turns.zh: 我从经理那里学到的一个非常有效的工具是，当你试图决定是否解雇某人或调整项目（即使这会让某人不满）时，问自己：“好吧，如果没有情感因素，如果这个人对此没有负面反应，我会怎么做？”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then that's the thing you should do and then you just do it. And then the question is how do I communicate this to them where their pain is lowest essentially.
turns.zh: 然后你就按这个做就行了。关键在于如何以最温和的方式把这个消息传达给他们，让他们感受到最小的痛苦。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: In the kindest way possible.
turns.zh: 用最温和的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the kindest way possible. And because, to your point, if you optimize for the other thing of making people feel good, everything just falls apart, they're going to suffer even more down the road.
turns.zh: 用尽可能委婉的方式说吧。因为，正如你所指出的，如果你一味追求让人们感觉良好的目标，最终一切都会分崩离析，他们日后只会遭受更大的痛苦。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. Direct is kind. And it feels kind or, really, honestly, easy to avoid these things or to work around them or to not but, at the end of the day, it's basically just a drag, the barnacle thing. It drags on your company, on your time, on your energy, et cetera.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对正确。直接行事更善良。但说实话，要避免这些问题、找到解决办法或者不去理会它们实在太难了。归根结底，这就像船上长出来的藤壶一样，拖累公司、浪费时间、消耗精力等等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. But again, very hard to do in real life to do the thing that's hard and cause someone to be sad and upset and frustrated and maybe leave.
turns.zh: 是啊。但说真的，在现实生活中要做到这些很难——既要面对困难，又可能让别人难过、生气甚至离开。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: It is so hard and all these things are muscles, you get better at ... They don't become easy, it's not like anybody who's like, "Oh, it's so ... I enjoy firing people," no, but you recognize it faster and you are like, "Oh, I need to go do this." And that is actually ... It's a practice and something that you need to practice to become the kind of leader that leads these long-enduring companies.
turns.zh: 这确实很困难，而所有这些技能都需要不断磨练。它们不会变得简单——没人会说“哦，这太容易了”之类的话，但你会更快意识到问题所在，然后想：“好吧，我需要去处理这件事。”而这实际上……这是一种修行，是你成为能引领这些经久不衰的公司的领导者所必须实践的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And this tool of thinking, asking what would I do if there were no emotions involved and this person wouldn't be upset, it helps you realize, okay, I see, this actually doesn't make sense to just do it the easy way right now because it doesn't make sense.
turns.zh: 是啊。这套思维工具——设想如果没有情感因素介入，对方也不会生气或沮丧——能帮助你意识到，现在就选择简单处理方式其实毫无意义，因为这根本说不通。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, it strips away. It strips away the emotions.
turns.zh: 是啊，它能剥去情感的外衣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else I wanted to make sure we spent a little time on is you have another tidbit along these lines which is around putting most of your energy into high performers versus spending all your time people that need help, talk about that.
turns.zh: 还有一点我想重点强调的，就是要把大部分精力投入到高绩效员工身上，而不是把时间花在需要帮助的人身上。谈谈这个吧。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: As a leader, as a manager, you're running these teams and someone's struggling and it's very easy to get dragged into that and to end up spending a huge amount of energy on it but high performers are actually the future of your company. And if you think about it and if you've spent time on it, those are the folks where, if you invest your time and energy in them, you're going to get the 10x return that people talk about all the time in Silicon Valley. But what I've witnessed is that most people have a high performer and they just leave them alone, they're like, "That person's doing well so I'm just going to let them do their thing." And what I do when I have a high performer that's my favorite thing in the world is invest time and energy in them and basically build a whole system of working with them that is designed to draw out potential. And I would say there's two things here, one is it's really important to realize that our tendency-
turns.zh: 作为领导者、管理者，当团队里有人遇到困难时，很容易被卷入其中，最终耗费大量精力。但高绩效员工才是公司未来的希望。仔细想想，你会发现，如果你为他们投入时间和精力，就能获得硅谷常提到的10倍回报。但我观察到，大多数人面对高绩效员工时，往往放任不管，心想“那个人表现不错，就随他去吧”。而我面对高绩效员工时，最喜欢做的事就是投入时间和精力，为他们量身打造一个能激发潜能的合作体系。这里有两个关键点：首先，意识到我们的倾向性非常重要——

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: There's two things here. One is it's really important to realize that our tendency is to actually spend time on low performers and it is not a good use of your time. See the point about firing people. But the other thing is that actively investing in and developing high performers is something that's important to get good at as a leader because that is how you create these little rocket ships that end up... You'll manage someone who's just like a project manager and all of a sudden they're running a whole function inside the company eventually, but it's because you took time and energy to invest in them. And my basic way of doing that, not to... I could spend a long time on this, but I would just say is I run experiments. I basically develop a theory about someone, "I think this person is capable of this kind of thing." And then piece by piece, it doesn't have to be a whole job or whole project. It can just be an incremental experiment, "I'm going to see if they can do this with less guidance or support from me." (01:09:52): I'm going to give them a bigger project. I'm going to give them something with more visibility. I'm going to manage them less, oversee them less, whatever. All of those are experiments to basically test your theory and deepen your theory in terms of this person's potential and their ability to help the company. And you're basically, for me, what I'm doing is deeply getting to know that person and then trying to pair them with company needs. What do we need? This person is great at zebra farming. Where do we need zebra farming? So how do I get them working on bigger and bigger and more and more critical things? (01:10:27): And to be honest, this is what people have done for me. At Facebook in particular, I've benefited from people being like, "Ooh, come help me with this thing." They saw potential in me and they asked me to help with something and it unlocked a huge amount for me. And so, it is such a powerful tool for getting more out of people that might be a little bit stuck if you leave them in this box. But if you start to expand the box, you can really unlock people.
turns.zh: 讲到这里，有两点需要强调。第一点是，我们必须意识到自己往往会把时间花在表现不佳的员工身上，而这其实是在浪费时间。这就是为什么要裁员的道理。但另一方面，积极投资和培养表现出色的员工，对于领导者而言至关重要，因为这样才能打造出能快速成长的"火箭飞船"。举个例子，你可能管理过一个项目经理级别的员工，最终却让他负责公司某个部门的全面运营。这就是因为你投入了时间和精力去培养他。我的方法不是一味强调这个，而是通过实践验证。具体来说，我会制定一个假设，比如"我认为这个人有潜力做成这件事"，然后逐步推进，不必一次性交付整个项目。可以先做一个渐进式实验，比如"看看他们在我的指导下能否独立完成任务"，或者"给他们一个更具挑战性的项目"、"赋予他们更高的可见度"、"减少对他们的微观管理"等等。这些都是验证假设、深化对员工潜力的认知，并帮助他们为公司创造价值的试验。对我来说，关键在于深入了解员工的能力，并将他们的特长与公司需求对接。比如，某位员工擅长"斑马式创新"，我们又在哪些领域需要这种创新思维？如何让他承担更重大、更关键的任务？（01:09:52）：说实话，这正是别人为我创造的机会。尤其是在Facebook，人们常主动邀请我参与项目，他们看到了我的潜力，赋予我更多责任，这让我获得了巨大的成长空间。这表明，当员工陷入某种思维定式时，拓宽他们的视野和责任边界能激发他们的潜能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So speaking of high performers, you've worked with many very high performing founder-CEOs. He worked really closely with Zuck, with Cheryl Sandberg, with Larry and Sergei at Google, with Brett Taylor, who I just... Just like you trying to read his resume, it takes three lines of things he's done over the course of his career. And so I just want to spend a little time on what are some things you've learned, maybe a few things you've learned from them, that group that you find yourself sharing with other people most.
turns.zh: 谈到高绩效员工，你与许多表现卓越的创始人兼CEO合作过。比如扎克伯格、谢丽尔·桑德伯格、谷歌的拉里和谢尔盖，还有布雷特·泰勒。光是看他的履历，仅三行字就概括了他职业生涯的成就。我想花点时间谈谈你从他们身上学到的东西，以及最常与他人分享的经验。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: That list is very long, but I'll give you a couple. The first one that I think is kind of counterintuitive is... So I said I worked at Facebook. I worked on culture, which is one of those words that doesn't really mean anything. So I define it as the way we do things around here. And I thought my job was to shape the culture. I thought it was to push the culture. And the most humbling lesson I learned is 80% of the culture of a company is literally defined by the personality of the founder. Facebook is Mark. Google is Larry and Sergei. Google, when I was there, it felt like a university. It's where ideas are more important in a lot of ways than what's shipped. And there's a campus and they basically wanted people to live there when I was there. It was designed to basically be a two PhD students' paradise. (01:12:29): Facebook felt like a 19-year-old hacker's dorm room when I was there. And it was shipping above all and all else. And it seeped with Mark's DNA. And I spent ages trying to create various changes inside the company or trying to push a point. And Mark would say literally one thing in an all hands, and it was like somebody threw a boulder into the pond. So our job as operators or as leaders around founders is to help articulate the culture that they're creating and to help extend it. My version of founder mode, which I know you've spent some time on on this podcast is your job is to build a company that would make a decision the way the founder would when they're not in the room. That is the work of building a company around a founder, but your job is not to shape culture. (01:13:24): That is mostly defined by the literal personality strengths and weaknesses of the person at the top. And that's been true of Mark and it's been true of Brett. Everywhere I go, that's who it is. You don't need a consulting firm to tell you, just go do a personality diagnosis on your founder. And the weaknesses thing is real. I've seen and watched friends try to shape a set of values at a company and it just doesn't match who the founder is. You say, "Move fast and break things," or whatever your version of that is. And your founder loves ambiguity and is perfectly happy with not making decisions. All that leads to is cultural dissonance. It leads to people being like, "Wait, what? I thought we said we care about moving fast and making aggressive decisions and it turns out..." So being really careful about what you say, because what people actually feel when it comes to culture is what you do and how you act every day. (01:14:18): You can never write anything down and you will still have a culture. It will be created through the actions and the decisions that you make and that your founder makes. So that would be a huge one.
turns.zh: 那个清单很长，但我可以举几个例子。第一个我觉得有点违背直觉的例子是……我说我在Facebook工作过。我负责的是企业文化建设，但这个词其实没什么实际意义。所以我把它定义为我们在这里做事的方式。我以为我的工作是塑造文化、推动文化进程。但我学到的最深刻的一课是，公司文化80%是由创始人的个性所决定的。Facebook就是马克，谷歌就是拉里和谢尔盖。我在谷歌工作时，那里感觉像一所大学。在那里，想法比产品交付更重要。谷歌有校园文化，鼓励员工住在园区里，简直就是两个博士生的天堂。（01:12:29）而Facebook在我那里时，感觉像个19岁黑客的宿舍，什么都追求快速交付，处处渗透着马克的个人风格。我花了很长时间试图在公司内部推动变革或强推某个观点，但马克在全体会议上说一句简单的话，就能引发轩然大波。所以作为创始人身边的运营者或领导者，我们的职责是帮助阐释他们正在塑造的文化，并将其延续下去。我提到的"创始人模式"（我知道你们在播客中也深入探讨过）就是，你要建立一个即使创始人不在场也能按照其决策方式运作的公司。这是围绕创始人打造公司的过程，但你的职责不是塑造文化。（01:13:24）文化主要由高层的个人特质决定，无论是优点还是缺点。马克如此，布雷特亦然。无论我在哪里工作，都能看到这种情况。根本不需要咨询公司来告诉你，直接给创始人做个性格诊断就行了。缺点是真实存在的。我见过朋友们试图在公司塑造一套价值观，结果却与创始人格格不入。你说“快速行动、勇于破坏”之类的，但创始人却喜欢模糊性，对做决策毫无兴趣。结果只能导致文化不和谐，人们会困惑：“等等，什么？我们不是说要快速行动、积极决策吗？结果……”。所以要格外谨慎自己的言行，因为人们对文化的真实感受，源自你每天的行动和处事方式。（01:14:18）你再怎么写文件，也无法完全塑造文化。文化最终会通过你的行动和决策，以及创始人的决策而形成。所以这才是最重要的一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me spend a little more time on this because this is so good. So all this advice on culture and it feels so true based on everything I've seen. So tip one there is just you can't really change the culture. Maybe there's a little bit on the edges you could adjust. It will come down and trickle down from the founder, CEO probably mostly, but just the founders in general.
turns.zh: 让我再多说几句，因为这太棒了。所以所有关于文化的建议，基于我的观察都非常有道理。所以第一条建议就是，你其实无法真正改变文化。或许边缘部分可以调整，但最终还是会从创始人那里渗透下来，可能主要是CEO，但总体而言都是创始人。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: And founder-CEO is probably the single biggest.
turns.zh: 而创始人-CEO可能是最大的影响因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Founder-CEO.
turns.zh: 创始人-CEO。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Co-founders, it depends a lot on the company.
turns.zh: 联合创始人，这取决于公司本身。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I think Stripe is probably very much like Patrick and John, but it's not every co-founder that has that level of power [inaudible 01:15:03].
turns.zh: 我觉得Stripe可能和帕特里克、约翰很像，但并非每位联合创始人都能拥有那样的权力（01:15:03，语音不清）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And then the way you describe culture, I think it's the way Seth Godin talks about it too, who's also been on the podcast. How cool is that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。然后你描述文化的方式，我觉得赛斯·高汀（Seth Godin）谈论文化的方式也和你很像，他也上过我们的播客。太酷了！

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: So cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He said, "Culture is..." And what you said, "Culture is the way we do things around here. That's what culture is, is how we..." That's how people describe your culture is, "The way we do things around here."
turns.zh: 他说：“文化就是……” 而你说：“文化就是我们在这里做事的方式。文化就是我们如何……” 人们描述你们文化的方式就是：“我们在这里做事的方式。”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I ran culture, whatever the hell that means, at Facebook for a hot second. I literally haven't done a values exercise since. And it sounds crazy, right? Because in theory, I know how to do this stuff. I don't really know how to do this stuff. But for me, the point is process and systems and how do we make decisions? That's where culture actually lives. It is what you do. It's how you hire. It's how you fire. It's who you don't hire. It's all of those decisions. That is culture. So whenever I'm working with a company or building a company, that's what I'm focused on, not on what's the shiny word that we're putting on the wall. You know what I mean?
turns.zh: 我在Facebook短暂负责过文化部门，不知道怎么回事，从那以后就再也没做过价值观评估了。听起来很疯狂，对吧？因为理论上我知道怎么做这些事。但实际上我真不知道怎么做。但对我来说，重点在于流程和制度，以及如何做决策？这才是文化真正存在的地方。它体现在你的行动中——招聘方式、解雇标准、拒绝录用的人选……所有这些决策才是文化。所以无论我是在和一家公司合作还是创办一家公司，我关注的都是这些，而不是墙上挂着的那些华丽词汇。你懂我的意思吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So the way you're describing is, as you said, it's what you do. It's not what you say?
turns.zh: 是的。所以你描述的文化，正如你所说，就是行动，而不是说辞？

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Keep going.
turns.zh: 太棒了。继续。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: I'll give you two more that are helpful. This one is a Mark Zuckerberg classic, but he has this very strong feeling that people don't escalate enough. And he was very adamant about it at Facebook. And he brought it to CZI too where he was like, "Escalation is a tool." And he's like, "People get stuck. They get stuck with two people with equal power trying to solve a problem. You can spend so much time bashing heads, going back and forth. And actually what you just need to do is go up. You need to go." The problem is that we think of escalation as, "I'm A and B and I are disagreeing. And so, I'm going to go up to C and tell on B. I'm going to go tattle to the teacher." That is not what escalation is. What escalation is, "We disagree. Neither one of us has enough power to make this decision. Let's go to someone who does." My boss, my boss's boss, whoever it is. (01:16:59): As soon as you are stuck, escalate. Go together, go make your case to whoever it is, go together up. That is unlocking. It's saving you a whole bunch of time. And it's something that I've found as I've worked with companies and leaders in Glue Club. It's not a muscle that's very comfortable for people, but it's so smart. And Mark has a lot of these, but that one I really took away because again, I think so many people think of escalation as bad, a failure, like, "I failed, so I had to escalate." No, it's a tool. It's what management is for. They're there to unblock you. Let them unblock you. Stop arguing over something you can't decide.
turns.zh: 我再给你两个很有用的建议。第一个是马克·扎克伯格（Mark Zuckerberg）的经典观点，但他坚信人们不常升级汇报渠道。他在Facebook就非常坚持这一点。他把这种理念带到CZI，也曾说：“升级汇报是工具。” 他说：“人们会陷入僵局。两个权力相当的人试图解决问题时，可能会陷入反复争执。这时你只需要向上汇报。” 问题是我们通常把升级汇报理解为“我和A、B意见不合，于是去找C告状”，但这不是升级汇报的正确理解。升级汇报应该是：“我们意见不合，两人都无法做决策，那就找有权力的人裁决。” 比如我的上司、上司的上司，无论是谁。（01:16:59）只要陷入僵局，就应该升级汇报。一起去找裁决者陈述观点，共同汇报。这才是破局之道。能为你节省大量时间。我在Glue Club与多家公司和领导者合作时发现，这并非人们乐意使用的工具，但确实高明。马克有很多类似的观点，但这个观点对我触动最深，因为我认为太多人把升级汇报视为失败、负面行为，比如“我失败了，所以不得不升级汇报。” 不，这只是一种工具。这才是管理的意义所在。他们存在的意义就是为你排忧解难。别再为无法决策的事争执不下了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they'll be so happy knowing you did not waste a week debating this and then just arguing and just looking at data. It's like, "Okay, I can just tell you exactly what we should do. Let's go do that."
turns.zh: 他们会很开心，因为知道你没有花一周时间争论不休，最后只是看看数据。就像：“好吧，我直接告诉你们该怎么做。咱们就去执行吧。”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Exactly. You lack context or you lack power. And then the last one actually is from Cheryl Sandberg, who I learned an enormous amount from, huge, was like going to business school without going to business school working with her. But I say it a lot right now, so I'm going to say it on your podcast so maybe some people will hear me. Growing more than 100% every year is a bad idea. The happiest growth rate is 50%, 100% is manageable. Anything more than doubling and you are signing yourself up for a world of pain. And I have seen this over and over and over again. I had to scream way louder about it five years ago than I do now because we've been through collectively a lot of pain and a lot of layoffs. And obviously the combination of 2021 and then AI has led us to talk about unit economics and scaling with tools, not people. (01:18:47): But I still see companies and I'm still talking to founders that are like, "Yeah, we're 50 people and we're going to be 150 people next year." And I'm like, "Could you possibly do that with 100 people?" But here's what basically happens if you grow at more than 100%, which is you're growing too fast to de-dupe all the issues. So somebody posts this role, it actually turns out that that role is also being hired for on this other team. So you're hiring two people who more or less have the same job description and are assigned to the same number or the same problem, but nobody talked to each other. And those two people both show up and they're like, "I am doing this." And the person's like, "Wait, I thought I was doing that." Anyway, so then you've got all this... And think about all the time and all the energy and all the money that goes into de-duping that. (01:19:32): If you slow down, if you hire for quality and for real need versus the panic hiring, whatever your sales model spits out or whatever, you'll actually find leverage. You find, "Oh, I didn't need that person," or, "I didn't need this whole team," or, "I didn't need this whole function," or, "I can wait for that." So slow down. And again, these are all just guidelines in terms of the 50% is happy and 100% is manageable. But having seen enough of this, I can tell you these are good rules and you should pay attention to them. And sometimes you're like, "I have to double or I have to more than double or I have to triple," or whatever. I'm like, "Okay, just ask a whole lot of questions as you open roles. Ask a whole lot of questions as you hire because you will find duplication, you will find chaos coming in the front door." (01:20:16): More people does not actually make you faster. Do you know what I mean? We think it does. It does not. It makes it harder. It makes it harder to get work done. It makes it slower. So you should be scared of adding people, not like, "Oh, this is the answer to all my problems."
turns.zh: 确实如此。要么是缺乏上下文，要么是缺乏执行力。最后这句话来自谢丽尔·桑德伯格，我从她身上学到了很多东西。和她共事就像是无需上商学院就能获得商业教育。但我现在经常说这些，所以我要在你的播客上再重复一遍，也许能让更多人听到。每年增长超过100%是个糟糕的主意。最理想的增长率是50%，100%还算可控。但增长超过一倍，你就是在给自己招来无穷的痛苦。我已经反复见证过无数次这种情况了。五年前我不得不更强烈地强调这个问题，因为我们共同经历了太多的痛苦和裁员。而2021年和人工智能的结合，让我们开始谈论单位经济学和用工具而非人力来实现规模化。（01:18:47）但我现在还是看到很多公司，仍然有创始人说：“是啊，我们现在有50人，明年要扩到150人。”我就会问：“你用100人就能做到吗？”但如果增长超过100%，问题就来了。因为你增长得太快，根本来不及解决所有问题。比如某个职位发布后，结果发现另一个团队也在招同样的职位。这时候就会有两个员工几乎拥有相同的职位描述，被分配到同一个部门或处理同一个问题，却根本没有沟通。结果两人同时到岗，都说：“这活儿我来做。”而负责人却说：“等等，我以为那活儿是我负责的。” 总之，解决这些问题要耗费大量时间、精力和资金。（01:19:32）如果你放慢节奏，根据实际需求而非恐慌式招聘来衡量质量，你就能找到真正的增长点。比如你会发现：“哦，这个岗位其实不需要这个人。”或者：“我们根本不需要整个团队。”或者：“这个部门可以等等。”所以慢下来。再说一次，这些都是50%可控、100%可控的指导方针。但经历得多了，就会发现这些规则很有效，你应该重视它们。有时候你会想：“我必须翻倍增长，或者超过翻倍，或者三倍增长。”但我会说：“好吧，在开放职位时多问问题，招聘时多提问，这样才能避免重复工作，避免混乱从源头产生。”（01:20:16）增加人手并不会让你效率更高。懂我的意思吗？我们以为会。但其实适得其反。它只会让工作更困难、更拖沓。所以要警惕增加人手，而不是把它当作解决所有问题的灵丹妙药。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And just to be clear, you're talking about the growth of the company. So doubling in a year, bad idea. It's possible, but you're saying it's going to be very hard and painful and probably a really bad idea.
turns.zh: 太棒了。再明确一点，你说的是公司的增长。所以一年翻倍，糟糕的主意。可能做到，但代价巨大。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah. More than doubling head count growth.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: More than doubling.

turns.en: Great point.
turns.zh: 说得好。

turns.en: Head count?
turns.zh: 人手数量？

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. It's-
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Please feel free to do whatever you want with your business.
turns.zh: 请随意处置你的业务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just advice. This is top of mind because I just had the interview with Matt McGinnis, but so much of what he talked about is this resonates with what you're talking about. He talked a lot about under-resourcing your team-
turns.zh: 只是个建议。这件事最近让我印象深刻，因为我刚和马特·麦金尼斯做了个采访，但他提到的很多观点都和您正在讨论的内容不谋而合。他谈了很多关于团队资源不足的问题——

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全同意。

turns.en: Leads to much better outcomes because people don't work on the low priority stuff. They focus on only high priority stuff. And the other is this idea of escalating. He talked a lot about that. Just like, "Escalation is good. Tell me when there's something I can help with, please. I'm here waiting constantly-
turns.zh: 这能带来更好的成果，因为人们不会去处理低优先级的任务。他们只专注于高优先级的事情。另一个观点是关于升级处理机制的。他对此讲了很多。比如，“升级请求是件好事。遇到需要我帮忙的地方，请随时告知。我会一直等着——”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 说得太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "To help."
turns.zh: “提供帮助。”

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Yeah, 100%.
turns.zh: 是啊，完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So maybe for a final question, one of your former colleagues, Eric Antonow, who's just this epic dude that few people know about-
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后再问个问题，你的前同事埃里克·安东诺夫——他是个很了不起的人，却鲜为人知——

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That I've chatted with over the last few months because he knows so many people that come on this podcast. He's a former Facebook person, now at OpenAI. I asked him what I should ask you about and he told me something really insightful about you. He said that you had this really massive growth spurt at Facebook, which you shared and talked about. And then after you leaving, you had this huge ambition to become COO, CEO, become this huge big deal boss person, just take over the world. And then he noticed your ambitions significantly pivot to working on community building and helping people with their careers. And you turned down really big C-level role opportunities. And the way he described it is you were a dog that once thought you were cat. And the other metaphor he used is you change from AC current to DC current, which I don't know exactly what that means. So does this resonate? And if so, just what happened there?
turns.zh: 过去几个月我和他聊过天，因为他认识很多上过这个播客的人。他曾是Facebook员工，现在在OpenAI工作。我问他该问您什么问题，他给了我个很有启发的见解。他说您在Facebook时曾经历过巨大的成长高峰，您分享过这段经历。离开Facebook后，您曾雄心勃勃想成为COO、CEO，统领整个行业。但后来他注意到您的职业方向发生了显著转变，转向社区建设和帮助他人职业发展，还拒绝了许多高层职位机会。他用了两个比喻：一是您曾以为自己是猫，结果却发现自己是狗；二是您从交流电转变为直流电。我不太明白这两个比喻的具体含义。您对此有何感触？如果有的话，具体发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Eric is actually better at metaphors than I am, and I regularly rip his metaphors. But yes, Eric Antonow, the least well-known, but most brilliant person in my life. So I gave a talk at a company recently and somebody asked the question, "What's something you've changed your mind about?" And I was like, "Woof." But I actually talked about this because... So my brain is developing this model that is not done yet, but it's basically this idea that everybody has a proving phase to their career where you're proving to yourself and probably to your parents and some other people that you're good at stuff. You're like, "I'm going to prove." And it's an important phase because you need to learn. All the stuff we talked about. You need to learn what you're good at. You need to learn that you are good at things and that people should hire you for things and what are those things? (01:23:22): But part of that phase is also doing what you think matters, what you think you should do. Family programming or career books tell you this is what you should do, titles and all that stuff. And then, I think everybody has a moment and I think this moment varies wildly in terms of when it hits people, where you hit some sort of wall or I don't know what it is, speed bump, something, and the world forces you to say, "Okay, I've proven myself and I'm good at this thing. What do I want to do with it?" And for me, I spent 10 or 15 years proving to myself and to others that I was really good at this thing, basically working with brilliant founders to help bring their vision to life, "That's what you should hire me to do." That's what I was known for. (01:24:20): And it turned out that that wasn't what I love doing anymore. And it was really, really hard to walk away from because there was a lot of shoulds. It was like, "You should take this job with this fancy title. People are going to think you're so cool." And you get to... I call it a LinkedIn crush where you're really excited to post the job on LinkedIn, but you're deeply unexcited about doing the job. So you have all these LinkedIn crushes and you're like... And I vividly remember this one job that I turned down where I had to go for many walks. And what I was repeating over and over again to myself was, "What does this get you that you don't already have? What does this get you that you don't already have?" And I think, for me, it was this realization that these things that fed me early in my career just didn't feed me anymore, that I didn't get joy and excitement out of doing these jobs anymore, and I wasn't scared. (01:25:20): So it led me actually on a very long, windy journey, a founder journey, even though I have trouble with that title, just like the influencer title, to figure out what I wanted to build. And what I would've told you I wanted to build three years ago is actually not what I'm doing today, but through a lot of really fun experiments and a journey that never ends, what I've discovered is that what I love doing is building safe spaces for leaders to learn and grow, but also to find sanity and connection in a world that's kind of insane, whether it's working in a startup or some other kind of insanity, but that feeds me and there's nothing I love more than that, and I could not have told you that three years ago, but, to Eric's point, it really took a lot of work to switch currents or switch myself from a dog to a cat or whatever his metaphor is. And I think it's the work of it's ongoing work, but it's that thing of what do I want versus what do I think people expect of me?
turns.zh: 埃里克实际上比我更擅长比喻，我经常拿他的比喻开玩笑。不过说真的，埃里克·安东诺夫是我生命中最不为人知却最具才华的人。最近我在一家公司做演讲，有人问我：“你曾改变过主意的事情是什么？” 我当时脱口而出：“哇哦。” 但我之所以提到这件事，是因为……我的大脑正在构建一个尚未完善的模型。这个模型主要认为，每个人的职业生涯都有一个证明阶段——你要向自己证明，向父母和其他人证明自己擅长某些事情。你会说：“我要证明自己。” 这个阶段很重要，因为你需要学习。我们之前讨论过的所有东西，你都需要去掌握自己的专长，并意识到自己确实擅长某些事情，人们应该雇佣你做这些事情。但问题是，这个阶段还需要你去做那些你认为重要的事情，那些家人和职业规划书告诉你应该做的事情——头衔之类的。然后，我觉得每个人都会经历一个转折点，这个转折点因人而异，可能是撞上某个障碍，或者遇到某种挑战，世界迫使你停下来问：“好吧，我已经证明了自己，擅长这些事情了。那我要用它们做什么？” 对我来说，我花了10到15年的时间向自己和他人证明我真的擅长某件事——基本上就是和优秀的创始人合作，将他们的愿景变为现实，“这就是你应该被雇佣做的事情。” 这就是我被认可的部分。（01:24:20）但结果发现，这不再是我热爱的事情了。要离开真的很艰难，因为到处都是“应该”和“必须”。比如，“你应该接受这份带有光鲜头衔的工作，人们会觉得你很酷。” 然后你得到……我称之为领英上的“心动时刻”——你真的很兴奋能在领英上发布这份工作，但对实际工作却毫无热情。所以你经历了无数次这样的心动时刻，然后你会问……我清楚记得拒绝过的一份工作，需要经常外出散步。我当时不断在心里问：“这能给你带来什么你已经有的东西？这能给你带来什么你已经有的东西？” 对我来说，关键在于意识到早期职业生涯中那些曾滋养我的东西，现在已不再对我有效了。我不再从这些工作中获得快乐和激情，但我并不害怕。（01:25:20）这实际上让我踏上了一段漫长而曲折的创业之旅，尽管我对这个头衔也感到棘手，就像对“网红”头衔一样。我需要弄清楚自己想创造什么。三年前我告诉你我想创造的东西，和今天做的不一样。但通过许多有趣的实验和永无止境的探索，我发现自己热爱的事情是为领导者搭建安全的学习和成长空间，让他们在疯狂的世界中找到理性和连接，无论是在创业公司工作，还是其他种类的疯狂环境中。但这滋养着我，没有什么比这更让我热爱了。三年前我无法预料到这一点，但正如埃里克所说，要改变方向，或者从“狗”变成“猫”（无论他的比喻是什么），真的需要付出大量努力。这是一项持续的工作，关键在于我想要什么，而不是别人期望我做什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so much depth there. This could be another entire podcast conversation talking through this journey, but I'm going to close with a note from your partner, Sarah. She told me that she has this sticker on her notebook with three pieces of advice that you gave her when she started at OpenAI. Get to know your customer, they have the answer; be patient because everything is going to change; and just keep trying. turns.zh: 里面有太多的深意了。这本可以成为另一期播客，深入探讨这段历程，但今天我想以你的搭档莎拉（Sarah）的话作为结束。她告诉我，她的笔记本上贴着三条你给她的建议，适用于她刚加入OpenAI时。第一条是"了解你的客户，他们手握答案"；第二条是"保持耐心，因为一切都会变"；第三条是"继续尝试"。最后我想问一句，有没有类似的建议值得分享给听众，或者你还有什么想留给听众的呢？

turns.speaker: Molly Graham
turns.en: Part of what I think is so important to realize inside of scaling and changing companies and the world is some things will always be true. And I think OpenAI is extra special on that front. You have to find these guiding lights that get you through that storm. And I think it's sort of the same thing as "Serve the business, not the people." What are the things that will always be true? We are here to do this. We are here to serve the customer. (01:28:09): And then the other piece of the three things that she wrote down is, I think that we, as humans, we seek stability. Our brains would like things to stop changing. We would like things to stay the same. And that is just not a reality inside of companies that are growing and changing as fast as OpenAI or a lot of the companies today that are being built. So actually, you need to start to expect instability. You need to start to just assume things are going to change. Assume you're going to have a new boss in six months. I talk about this a lot when I talk to folks at OpenAI, "You need to stop expecting that anything's going to be the same in six months or a year. You will have a different job. You will have a different boss." (01:28:55): How do you prepare for that? Do you know what I mean? How do you almost see the instability as stability because it's the only thing that is definitely going to be true. And part of that is to just keep going. You know what I mean? To just find these lights and these compasses or whatever metaphor sticks with you and focus on those because whatever is happening around you, you just got to keep moving forward and keep learning as much as you can because that's the real opportunity. Whatever happens to the company, however successful it is, all that you take away from it... You might hopefully take a bunch of money, but you might not. So people and what you learned, that's it. Focus on that.
turns.zh:
在谈论规模化扩张、公司变革和世界变化时，有一点至关重要——有些真理永远不变。我对莎拉说"了解你的客户，他们手握答案"的意思是，无论你周围发生多少混乱，无论本周又有多少壁垒和天花板被重新调整，客户永远不会变。这是永恒不变的真理。我认为，在面对风暴般的规模化扩张和创业公司时，必须找到那些不变的指引灯，找到那些能带你穿越风暴的罗盘。OpenAI在这方面做得尤为出色。你必须找到那些能指引你前行的明灯。正如"为业务服务，而非为人服务"所言，哪些真理永恒不变？我们的使命就是服务客户。（01:28:09）  
她记下的另外三条建议中，我认为作为人类，我们追求稳定。大脑渴望事物停止变化，渴望一切保持原样。但在像OpenAI这样快速发展、日新月异的公司里，或者当今许多初创企业中，这根本不现实。所以你必须开始预期不稳定，必须假定一切都会变化。比如，六个月后你可能换个新老板。我在OpenAI内部常说："别指望六个月或一年后一切如故。你会有新工作、新老板。"（01:28:55）  
如何为此做好准备？你懂我的意思吗？如何把不稳定视为稳定，因为这是唯一确定不变的真理。关键在于坚持前行。你懂我的意思吧？找到那些指引灯，专注于它们，因为无论周围发生什么，你都要继续前进，尽可能多地学习，这才是真正的机遇。无论公司成功与否，你能从中收获的都是喜欢与你共事、愿意再次合作的人，以及你学到的知识。仅此而已。或许你能赚很多钱，或许不能。但人脉和所学，才是最宝贵的财富。专注于这些。
